variants.name: In-out parameter (collect(into: &out))
variants.implementation_notes: Swift's explicit output parameter is `inout`: `func collect(_ node: Node, into out: inout [String])` appends with `out.append(...)` and the caller passes `&accumulator`. The value is passed in, modified and written back out, and exclusivity checking rejects overlapping accesses, so accidental aliasing of the same accumulator fails fast instead of corrupting results. The stdlib's sink-protocol form is `TextOutputStream` with `print(_:to:)` (see variants); for text, returning a `String` built by interpolation is usually simpler.
pitfalls: Passing the same variable to two `inout` parameters, or re-entering the function while it is borrowed, is an exclusivity violation - a compile-time error or a runtime trap, not silent corruption.

`inout` copies in and writes back for non-trivial types: a large accumulator can be copied at the call boundary where a class reference would be cheaper (the copy is also what prevents aliasing bugs).
Mutating the collection while iterating it (a producer appending to the same array it is walking) invalidates the iteration.

variants.name: TextOutputStream sink (print(_:to:))
variants.idiom_name: TextOutputStream conformance passed inout to print(_:to:)
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library ships the pattern as a sink protocol: conform a type to `TextOutputStream` by implementing `mutating func write(_ string: String)`, then hand it to `print(_:to:)`/`dump(_:to:)`, which append their formatted output to that stream (String already conforms, so output can be captured into a string). This is the right realization when the producers are the stdlib's own printing functions or anything else that writes into a `TextOutputStream`; the protocol may call `write(_:)` several times per operation, so implementations must append only.
pitfalls: A `TextOutputStream` is passed `inout` and may be called several times per print: a value-type stream (struct) must implement `mutating func write` and is copied at the call boundary.
Writers that throw away the stream's identity (storing it, returning it, letting it escape) break the inout write-back contract the API depends on.
`print(_:to:)` adds separators and a terminator, so a stream intended to collect raw fragments receives 'label: value\n' shapes unless `separator`/`terminator` are overridden.
